editor_spans.body: Last week I described the Prime Minister's offer to Holyrood as a challenge more than a gift. The speech itself shows how he plans to get past the fact that Westminster does not control Scottish local government. What he can give away is something Westminster still controls: employment support run by the DWP. He calls this 'an offer of DWP devolution', and it is the only concrete power in a speech otherwise full of general talk about 'regional economic empowerment'. It also comes with a condition. The support must be built on the 'Easterhouse principle' of 'names not numbers', and 'if it's not based on that, it won't work'.

This deserves attention because it reverses the usual order of devolution. In 1999, and again with the Scotland Act 2016 (which devolved some employment programmes and led to Fair Start Scotland), powers went to Holyrood to use as it chose. This time a reserved power is offered with a model of how to use it attached, and that model is local and run from the bottom up. Holyrood would be taking money and powers from Westminster on the understanding that it passes them further down, to the same regions Burnham says it has starved. If the Scottish Government says no, it looks as if it is turning down jobs help for the one in six young Scots he says are not in education, employment or training. If it says yes, it accepts Westminster's account of its own centralisation. Either way the pressure is on Holyrood.

Underneath the politics there is a real argument, and it rests on a long history. The Ravenscraig and Leigh passages are not just scene-setting. They tell the story of deindustrialisation as a failure of where decisions were made: 'a decision taken hundreds of miles away' about places nobody consulted. That diagnosis applies to Edinburgh as much as to London. It explains why he lists Holyrood next to Westminster as a 'centre' and sets Dundee's one-in-five empty shops against Edinburgh's one in twenty. Ravenscraig closed in 1992. The SNP has said for a generation that Scotland's problems come from decisions taken in London, and that line works much less well against an argument that blames distance from power wherever it sits. That is why the speech is harder for Holyrood to answer than it first looks.

The things to watch are the National Economic Council meeting 'in a couple of weeks' and whether DWP devolution shows up there with real money and a timetable. The Defence Technical Excellence College deal, with £10m matched by each government, is the only joint result so far, and it is small. Burnham's Manchester record, where he controlled the buses and chose to buy them from Falkirk, shows he means it when he holds a lever himself. What Scotland has not yet seen is the UK centre actually giving levers away. Until a reserved budget actually moves, 'devolution by default' is only a slogan.

Story 509, the Editor's, made 2026-10-24: "The Prime Minister's 'offer' to Holyrood is really a challenge. Local government in Scotland is devolved, so Westminster has no power to hand Scottish regions anything. It can only shame the Scottish Government by calling it one of the most centralised in Europe. Andy Burnham is offering the city-region model that made his name in Manchester, delivered through No10 North and the Scotland Office. In effect it creates a second route by which Westminster can deal directly with Scottish regions. The Derby headquarters and the East Midlands mayor's comments come from the same playbook. Whether Scotland's First Minister accepts will show whether this is about governing or about positioning."; cited by no later Editor's Span
  S359 (the Editor's): The Prime Minister's 'offer' to Holyrood is really a challenge. Local government in Scotland is devolved, so Westminster has no power to hand Scottish regions anything. It can only shame the Scottish Government by calling it one of the most centralised in Europe. Andy Burnham is offering the city-region model that made his name in Manchester, delivered through No10 North and the Scotland Office. In effect it creates a second route by which Westminster can deal directly with Scottish regions. The Derby headquarters and the East Midlands mayor's comments come from the same playbook. Whether Scotland's First Minister accepts will show whether this is about governing or about positioning.
